assessment: The incumbent plausibly combines useful assembly verification with costly selection, insertion and packing, but their separate contributions are unmeasured. Repeated three-compartment orders took seven to nine minutes, whereas mixed batches contained every extreme delay: a limiting observation against assuming full assembly is inherently too slow. Layout complexity and batch switching remain confounded. Seventeen reinsertion events warrant investigation, but overlapping widths limit a simple width-only explanation. Customer reports suggest component errors without establishing their precise source; three observed short-partition questions suggest an instruction problem. These observations do not establish pilot success or justify changing geometry or connections.

openings.claim: Staging one order-specific set of parts with a count check before insertion may reduce mixed-layout delays and component errors.
openings.delta: Retains full assembly while replacing shared-bin selection during assembly with an explicit, individually checked kit.
openings.prediction: Against the incumbent at matched layout complexity, staging reduces total selection-plus-checking time and wrong-part events; insertion time need not improve.
openings.probe: Use twelve reusable sample organizers, four per compartment count. Both workers alternate methods with counterbalanced order. Time selection, insertion, checking and packing separately, including kit preparation, and record discrepancies before correction. Retain accepted colors and counts; adopt only if cost and delivery gates pass.
assumptions: Staging fits one bench, the delivery schedule and both cost caps.

openings.claim: A diagram specific to the ordered arrangement, explicitly locating the short partition, may improve unaided customer arrangement.
openings.delta: Replaces the three-layout diagram with an exact-order mapping while preserving supplied parts and rearrangeability.
openings.prediction: Short-partition placement errors and help requests decrease even if physical insertion retries persist.
openings.probe: Reuse verified complete sample sets. Assign the ten participants to matched five-person groups using either diagram; observe first attempts, placement errors, insertion retries and unaided completion. Treat results as directional, then verify the 60-unit targets separately.
assumptions: Ambiguous placement contributes to requests for help.
Diagram preparation and printing fit the time and cost constraints.
